__9DNgEJVqE.title: Moderation #3: Salman and Abu al-Darda
__9DNgEJVqE.one_line: Salman's visit to Abu al-Darda: your Lord, your family and your body each have a right, so give each its due.
__9DNgEJVqE.summary: The sheikh calls the story of Salman al-Farisi and Abu al-Darda one of the most powerful on moderation. The Prophet had paired them as brothers, Salman from the emigrants and Abu al-Darda from the Ansar. Visiting, Salman found Umm al-Darda neglected and was told her husband had no interest in worldly life. Abu al-Darda offered food but said he was fasting; Salman refused to eat until he ate. At night Salman twice told him to sleep, then woke him near dawn to pray together, and told him that his Lord, his family and his own self each have a right over him, so he must give each its due. When they went to the Prophet, he confirmed that Salman was right. The sheikh explains that Abu al-Darda had begun living without relations with his wife, fasting daily and praying all night to draw closer to Allah. Salman, a seasoned seeker who had travelled the earth in search of truth before Islam, recognised that this was not balanced. Being truly religious, the sheikh says, means honouring the rights of Allah, spouse, children, relatives and body together. He closes by reading the full narration from Bukhari.

outline.gist: Introduces the narration of Abu Juhayfah about the brotherhood the Prophet formed between Salman and Abu al-Darda.

outline.heading: Abu al-Darda's imbalance and Salman's experience
outline.gist: Abu al-Darda had abandoned his wife for constant fasting and prayer; Salman, a lifelong seeker of truth, saw it was unbalanced.

outline.heading: Religiosity requires balance
outline.gist: The most religious person honours the rights of Allah, family, relatives and body together.

outline.heading: The Prophet confirms Salman
outline.gist: Abu al-Darda brings the matter to the Prophet, who affirms that extra worship without balance is not his way.

outline.heading: The full narration in Bukhari
outline.gist: He reads the complete hadith text as recorded by al-Bukhari.

kyokMpSBPIQ.speaker: adnan
kyokMpSBPIQ.speaker_note: his long-running Tuesday Tazkiyah self-value series, refers back to earlier weeks
kyokMpSBPIQ.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: Self-Value #38
kyokMpSBPIQ.one_line: The Quranic map of the self versus Freud and modern psychology, roles as a source of value, and the danger of deriving worth from religiosity.
kyokMpSBPIQ.summary: The sheikh completes his Quranic nomenclature of the self. The ruh is the real you, the part capable of empathy and sacrifice; the nafs's great trick is convincing you that its urges are yours. He defines the fu'ad as consciousness, the 'aql as reasoning, the subconscious as a mixing pot that absorbs one's environment, which is why company, media and sitting with scholars shape character at any age, and the damir as the conscience, whose strength mirrors the ruh against the nafs. He contrasts this with Freud's ego, id and superego and with CBT, IFS and trait theories, which change behaviour but ignore the why and leave out the Creator. Human value is divine and constant; the nafs, rooted in earthly survival, is not evil but must be educated rather than killed. He then names two more false sources of value. Diversifying roles is safe but unhealthy, as empty nesters and children who lose a friend show. Worst is deriving worth from religiosity: one then despairs after sin, which is Shaytan's first trick, and looks down on others, and may even resent someone closer to Allah. Good deeds are gifts from Allah done out of fear, hope or love; we rely on His mercy, walking a path rather than chasing a score. This introduces the coming study of vanity and arrogance.

outline.heading: Opening
Completing the Quranic nomenclature
outline.gist: Self-value drives almost everything; the Quran and Sunnah offer precise terms forming a complete psychological framework.

outline.heading: Psychology without a Creator
outline.gist: Freudian and modern psychology see man as a sophisticated mammal only, which is why culturally and religiously sensitive approaches have grown.

outline.heading: The Quran's terms are not interchangeable
outline.gist: Each word names a specific structure of the self, and knowing them lets you enjoy the Quranic narrative.

outline.heading: The ruh: the real you
outline.gist: The ruh comes from Allah and is capable of empathy, kindness and selflessness; the nafs's biggest trick is convincing you that you and it are the same.

outline.heading: What you want versus what the nafs wants
outline.gist: Both are part of you, but their wants differ because they see the world differently.

outline.heading: Fu'ad and 'aql: consciousness and intellect
outline.gist: The fu'ad receives all sensory experience; the 'aql reasons from premises to conclusions.

outline.heading: The subconscious as a mixing pot
outline.gist: It absorbs everything in the background and produces emotions we cannot control directly but can influence through what we feed it.

outline.heading: Environment shapes behaviour
outline.gist: A child in a bad classroom changes, and years of music on public transport leave their mark whether we like it or not.

outline.heading: What films plant in the background
outline.gist: Viewers absorb the hero's surroundings and later chase the cars, lawns and houses without knowing why.

outline.heading: The morsel of flesh
outline.gist: If the heart is sound the whole body is sound; a subconscious full of garbage cannot enjoy the Quran or the masjid.

outline.heading: Why students stay close to their sheikh
outline.gist: Long companionship lets the subconscious absorb adab and character, just as bad company rubs off.

outline.heading: Even a seventy-year-old changes
outline.gist: Company shapes character at any age, for better or worse.

outline.heading: The damir: conscience
outline.gist: Conscience reflects the strength of the ruh against the nafs; when the nafs normalizes a sin guilt disappears, but this is reversible.

outline.heading: Freud's ego and id
outline.gist: Popular 'ego' means the arrogant nafs, while Freud's ego is the realistic mediator; his id parallels the nafs.

outline.heading: The superego
outline.gist: Freud's moral, perfection-seeking part has no clear Islamic parallel and is no longer used as a framework.

outline.heading: CBT, IFS and trait theories
outline.gist: Modern frameworks focus on behaviours and traits, IFS being closest to the Islamic view, but skip the why that sustains change.

outline.heading: The pendulum is how the nafs feels
outline.gist: Swinging value is the nafs's view; like untangling a bad marriage, we must separate ourselves from it.

outline.heading: Value is divine and constant
outline.gist: Being human never increases or decreases; worth rests on the constant potential to turn one's life around.

outline.heading: The nafs is rooted in survival, not evil
outline.gist: Born of earth's drive to survive, it wants superiority; it should be educated and controlled, never killed or hated.

outline.heading: Holding the middle is lifelong work
outline.gist: Attachments keep returning; staying confident and humble at once is a skill learned over time, with mortality as a key aid.

outline.heading: Roles as a source of value
outline.gist: Spreading worth across many roles protects against collapse, but losing a sole role, as empty nesters do, shows the danger.

outline.heading: Children, friends and why diversifying is unhealthy
outline.gist: Children can crumble when a friend shuns them; diversifying is safe but is a mask, since value was never up for debate.

outline.heading: The worst source: religiosity
outline.gist: Deriving worth from moral or religious superiority is the most problematic source of all.

outline.heading: Despair after sin: Shaytan's first trick
outline.gist: Ibn Ata'illah's first aphorism: relying on deeds shows in losing hope when you slip, which Shaytan exploits.

outline.heading: The spiral of sin
outline.gist: Sin lowers self-worth, which pushes one to sin again and drift further away.

outline.heading: Acceptable motives for good deeds
outline.gist: Fear of punishment, hope of reward and loyal love for Allah leave no reason to feel more or less after a deed.

outline.heading: Looking down on the non-religious
outline.gist: Basing worth on religiosity implies others are less worthy, a judgment non-religious people feel.

outline.heading: Using worship to feel better than others
outline.gist: The Quran's warnings about arrogance target mostly the religious who used piety to feel superior.

outline.heading: Deeds done to feel good are already rewarded
outline.gist: Worship done to boost self-esteem is not for Allah; the good feeling is its whole reward.

outline.heading: Depend on Allah's mercy, not your deeds
outline.gist: His mercy and our value never change; deeds express our desire for His mercy and move us toward reward.

outline.heading: No number of deeds earns Paradise
outline.gist: No one can say how many or what quality of deeds is enough, so no one can claim to deserve Paradise.

outline.heading: From achieving a goal to walking a path
outline.gist: A sinner may repent at the end and be saved, so each moment we simply try our best and repent when we fail.

outline.heading: Deeds as facilitation from Allah
outline.gist: Seeing worship as Allah enabling us, rather than as our achievement, prevents judging others and collapse after sin.

outline.heading: Never misuse the greatest gift
outline.gist: Using closeness to Allah to feel superior is so disrespectful that one risks losing it forever.

outline.heading: The module's real name: mercy and humility
outline.gist: In Arabic scholarship this module is a pillar of tazkiyah about rahma and tawadu'; self-value is his English framing.

outline.heading: Resenting someone more religious
outline.gist: If piety is your worth, a more pious person becomes a rival, which is worse than never having done a good deed.

outline.heading: Vanity and arrogance as defences of insecurity
outline.gist: The Quran addresses the swing toward superiority because it is a defence against feeling less.

outline.heading: Every act of worship recentres the pendulum
outline.gist: Coming sessions will show how salah, zakat and Quran are designed to bring the self back to the middle.

themes.label: Self-value, self-worth, confidence
themes.note: Worth is divine and constant; roles and especially religiosity are false sources of value.

themes.label: Islamic psychology and the structures of the self
themes.note: Ruh, nafs, fu'ad, 'aql, subconscious and damir compared with Freud, CBT, IFS and trait theories.

themes.label: Tazkiyah: purifying and training the self
themes.note: The nafs is educated and controlled, not killed; holding the middle is lifelong work.

themes.label: Brotherhood, companionship and friendship
themes.note: Company and environment are absorbed by the subconscious and shape character at any age.

themes.label: Hope, fear and the balance between them
themes.note: Relying on deeds breeds despair after sin; rely on Allah's mercy and act from fear, hope and love.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: Piety used to feel superior is the arrogance the Quran most warns about.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: Vanity and arrogance are defences of insecurity, the subject of coming sessions.

themes.label: Intention and sincerity (niyyah, ikhlas)
themes.note: Worship done to feel good about oneself is not done for Allah.

themes.label: Envy, anger and other diseases of the heart
themes.note: Resenting someone more religious than you.

quran.point: The Quran already established the honour of Adam and his descendants, so it moves on to vanity and arrogance.

hadith.gist: There is a morsel of flesh in the body; if it is sound the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt the whole body is corrupt: it is the heart.
No one enters Paradise by his deeds alone, but by Allah's mercy.
A person may do the deeds of the people of the Fire until the end is near, then turn and be among the people of Paradise, and the reverse.

maxims: The nafs's biggest trick: convincing you that it is you
Educate the nafs, do not kill it
Walking a path, not achieving a goal
Never derive a scent of value from good deeds
Confident and humble at the same time

stories.who: Ibn Ata'illah's first aphorism (al-Hikam)
stories.point: Losing hope when you sin shows reliance on deeds instead of on Allah.

contemporary: Freudian psychology: ego, id and superego
Cognitive behavioural therapy, internal family systems and trait theories of personality
Culturally sensitive approaches in psychotherapy
Films shaping aspirations for cars and big houses
Empty nest syndrome
takeaways: Separate your own wants from the urges of your nafs.
Guard your environment, media and company, since the subconscious absorbs them.
Do not let a sin drive you to despair; repent and rely on Allah's mercy.
See good deeds as Allah's gift, never as proof you are better than others.
Work daily at keeping your self-worth in the middle: confident and humble.

uVPKvN6SPDQ.speaker_note: presents the centralization framework he put out years ago; mentions his sons and that his work would be impossible where he grew up
uVPKvN6SPDQ.title: From Populations to Communities: Social Centralization
uVPKvN6SPDQ.one_line: Why Muslims in Canada must build shared identity, equality, protected norms and intermarriage to become a real community.
uVPKvN6SPDQ.summary: The sheikh argues that Muslims in Canada enjoy religious freedoms most Muslims lack, and that these freedoms carry the responsibility to protect and use them. The first step is to turn city populations into communities that later connect and speak with one voice, because three generations of unprotected integration leave only a small fraction practising, and attendance percentages are already near that mark. He restates his framework of four centralizations (social, financial, religious leadership and political) and, while he once only hoped for financial unity, now sketches the social one, drawing on the Prophet's move from Mecca to Medina. Living close together is the main ingredient but impractical, so he focuses on what can be built anyway. A shared social identity gives young people, who outgrow belonging only to their family, something bigger to belong to. Social equality means no family, ethnicity or language ranks above others, with Arabic valued only as the language of the Quran, so masjids do not split into ethnic silos. Communities must develop their own norms and protect them through social reward and disapproval. Finally, a community that does not intermarry is not a community, and rigid matching by village leaves many capable Muslims unmarried. He calls for champions to build these pieces.

outline.heading: Freedom in the West brings responsibility
outline.gist: Muslims in Canada have more religious freedom than almost anywhere, and must protect and use it.

outline.heading: First step: become communities, then connect
outline.gist: City populations must become communities that link up and unify their voice.

outline.heading: The three-generation warning
outline.gist: Unprotected integration leaves about 15 percent practising after three generations, as happened to other faiths; we are near it.

outline.heading: Four centralizations, finances first
outline.gist: Social, financial, religious leadership and political; he once only hoped for finances.

outline.heading: Sketching the full picture: Mecca and Medina
outline.gist: He presents what full centralization would look like, drawing parallels with the two periods.

outline.heading: Why Medina was needed
outline.gist: The Muslims of Mecca had the Prophet's religious leadership but could not centralize the rest.

outline.heading: Geographic proximity: the main piece
outline.gist: Living together builds much, but selling homes to cluster is unrealistic; being spread across London is also a blessing.

outline.heading: Proximity builds culture
outline.gist: The hijrah gathered Muslims in one place to build a culture, which every family, business or community needs.

outline.heading: Shared identity
outline.gist: Being Muslim is a social identity as well as a theology, like being Canadian; our youth are weak on it.

outline.heading: Why children need something bigger to belong to
outline.gist: Belonging to a family stops being enough; shared events and Eid together build identity, as the Prophet did for young companions.

outline.heading: Social equality
outline.gist: No family, nationality or language ranks higher; Arabic matters only as the Quran's language; ethnic masjids must not replace community.

outline.heading: Distance makes contempt easy
outline.gist: Like insulting other drivers, it is easy to belittle people who are not your neighbours.

outline.heading: Interlude
Developing norms
outline.gist: Custom ('urf) is a source of evidence; the community needs its own norms alongside each culture's.

outline.heading: Protecting norms
outline.gist: Social reward and disapproval restrain wrongdoing, which is why parents want to send children back home.

outline.heading: Marriage across groups
outline.gist: Marrying only from one's village leaves many capable Muslims single; compatibility (kafa'ah) can be set up across groups.

outline.heading: Outro

jJB5UFG_-zo.speaker_note: his voice and references: his Hajj preparation sessions, his teacher who memorized Jabir's hadith, Syrian origin, age 40
jJB5UFG_-zo.title: Fifth Annual Iftar: The Day of Arafah
jJB5UFG_-zo.one_line: On the Day of Arafah: Adam and Eve's moment of realization, and Jabir's loving account of the Prophet's farewell Hajj.
jJB5UFG_-zo.summary: Speaking at a Day of Arafah iftar, the sheikh links Arafah to ma'rifah: on that mount Adam and Eve came to know what they had done, who they were and who Allah is. Hajj begins there, and its only indispensable pillar is standing at Arafah, because the pilgrimage is really a journey inward. The lesson is to admit to yourself what you already know, without the self-justification people usually seek. He calls Arafah humanity's anniversary, the place our first parents properly met after time apart, which makes all people siblings and equal. Their separation from Paradise taught them to appreciate Allah, as people only value someone after losing them; true knowers know Allah through lived experience. He then completes his Hajj series with the third storyline, the Prophet's farewell Hajj, through Jabir's long narration in Muslim: the aged, blind Jabir touching the chest of the Prophet's great-grandson and talking for pages like a man in love, the crowds converging on Medina, the sea of people around the Prophet, his talbiyah restoring Hajj to humility, his du'a on Safa twenty years after being driven off it, and the revelation of the completion of the religion that told him his end was near. He urges people to notice beautiful moments while they are in them.

outline.heading: Arafah and ma'rifah: the day of realization
outline.gist: On the mount Adam and Eve realized what they had done and what Allah destined for them.

outline.heading: Hajj is Arafah
outline.gist: Everything else can be missed or made up, but without standing at Arafah there is no Hajj.

outline.heading: A journey to a place inside you
outline.gist: Hajj forces us back to the human story of mistake, guilt, realization and repentance.

outline.heading: You already know what is right
outline.gist: Without ego and emotion, people almost always know the right thing; the step is admitting it.

outline.heading: Take off the mask before yourself
outline.gist: We justify mistakes and seek agreement; Adam and Eve had no one to admit to but themselves.

outline.heading: Humanity's anniversary
outline.gist: Each year humanity returns to the very place its first parents were reunited in maturity.

outline.heading: Children of the same two parents
outline.gist: However different we look and live, no one belongs to Adam and Eve more than another.

outline.heading: Why Arafah is the best day of the year
outline.gist: It is where humanity's story began, when knowledge and realization entered.

outline.heading: Knowing someone anew after separation

outline.heading: Perhaps I will not meet you after this
outline.gist: His opening words silenced the crowd: this was his last great public address.

pYCsGiKyHXs.title: Moderation #2
pYCsGiKyHXs.one_line: The hadith warning against ghuluw in religion: why imbalance inside our religiosity is the most damaging kind and how to find the sweet spot.
pYCsGiKyHXs.summary: The sheikh continues his moderation series with a short hadith he wants people to memorize: the Prophet's warning, beware of ghuluw in the religion. He explains the opening word as a warning to stay away, and traces ghuluw to a root used for prices rising beyond what is affordable and water boiling until it loses control. Ghuluw is misjudging something's worth, giving it more or less than it deserves. Everyone misbalances parts of life, he says, and Islam exists to teach balance, but imbalance inside religiosity itself is the worst place for it. His example is reverence for the Prophet: fall below the proper respect, as the Quran warns about raising voices to him, and deeds lose their value; go beyond it and you repeat what was done with Isa. The right point is not a mathematical middle between two wrong answers but the correct answer itself. He describes people who overemphasize the mechanics of practice or the spirituality and end up walking through Islam with a limp. Finding the balance takes education, dedication and attention, and it is central to the religion.

outline.heading: Religion is the worst place to lose balance
outline.gist: Humans always misjudge priorities in life, but exaggeration inside the religion is the most harmful.

outline.heading: Reverence for the Prophet as a test of balance
outline.gist: Too little respect voids deeds, as with raising voices to him; too much repeats what was done with Isa.

outline.gist: The balanced answer is right in itself, not a midpoint between two wrong answers.

full.full_ar: يروي الإمام النسائي في سننه (3057) قال: أَخْبَرَنَا يَعْقُوبُ بْنُ إِبْرَاهِيمَ الدَّوْرَقِيُّ، قَالَ حَدَّثَنَا ابْنُ عُلَيَّةَ، قَالَ حَدَّثَنَا عَوْفٌ، قَالَ حَدَّثَنَا زِيَادُ بْنُ حُصَيْنٍ، عَنْ أَبِي الْعَالِيَةِ، قَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ: «قَالَ لِي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم غَدَاةَ الْعَقَبَةِ وَهُوَ عَلَى رَاحِلَتِهِ: هَاتِ الْقُطْ لِي. فَلَقَطْتُ لَهُ حَصَيَاتٍ هُنَّ حَصَى الْخَذْفِ، فَلَمَّا وَضَعْتُهُنَّ فِي يَدِهِ قَالَ: بِأَمْثَالِ هَؤُلاَءِ، وَإِيَّاكُمْ وَالْغُلُوَّ فِي الدِّينِ، فَإِنَّمَا أَهْلَكَ مَنْ كَانَ قَبْلَكُمُ الْغُلُوُّ فِي الدِّينِ»
full.full_en: Imam an-Nasa'i narrates in his Sunan (3057): Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim al-Dawraqi narrated to us from Ibn 'Ulayyah, from 'Awf, from Ziyad ibn Husayn, from Abu al-'Aliyah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "On the morning of al-'Aqabah, while he was on his mount, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Come, pick up [pebbles] for me.' So I picked up for him small pebbles, the size used for flicking. When I placed them in his hand he said: 'Like these. And beware of excess in religion, for those who came before you were destroyed only by excess in religion.'"
full.isnad_ar: أَخْبَرَنَا يَعْقُوبُ بْنُ إِبْرَاهِيمَ الدَّوْرَقِيُّ، قَالَ حَدَّثَنَا ابْنُ عُلَيَّةَ، قَالَ حَدَّثَنَا عَوْفٌ، قَالَ حَدَّثَنَا زِيَادُ بْنُ حُصَيْنٍ، عَنْ أَبِي الْعَالِيَةِ، قَالَ قَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ
full.isnad_en: Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim al-Dawraqi from Ibn 'Ulayyah from 'Awf from Ziyad ibn Husayn from Abu al-'Aliyah from Ibn 'Abbas
full.ar_block: يروي الإمام النسائي في سننه، بسند صحيح، عن عبد الله بن عباس رضي الله عنهما قال: «قَالَ لِي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم غَدَاةَ الْعَقَبَةِ وَهُوَ عَلَى رَاحِلَتِهِ: هَاتِ الْقُطْ لِي. فَلَقَطْتُ لَهُ حَصَيَاتٍ هُنَّ حَصَى الْخَذْفِ، فَلَمَّا وَضَعْتُهُنَّ فِي يَدِهِ قَالَ: بِأَمْثَالِ هَؤُلاَءِ، وَإِيَّاكُمْ وَالْغُلُوَّ فِي الدِّينِ، فَإِنَّمَا أَهْلَكَ مَنْ كَانَ قَبْلَكُمُ الْغُلُوُّ فِي الدِّينِ»
full.en_block: Imam an-Nasa'i narrates in his Sunan, with an authentic chain, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "On the morning of al-'Aqabah, while he was on his mount, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Come, pick up [pebbles] for me.' So I picked up for him small pebbles, the size used for flicking. When I placed them in his hand he said: 'Like these. And beware of excess in religion, for those who came before you were destroyed only by excess in religion.'"
full.grade: Sahih. Graded sahih by al-Albani and Zubair 'Ali Za'i (isnad sahih); authenticated by Ibn Khuzaymah (2867), Ibn Hibban (3871) and Ibn al-Jarud; al-Hakim said it meets the conditions of al-Bukhari and Muslim and al-Dhahabi agreed.
full.note: Said while picking pebbles for stoning the Jamrah at Hajj. Ibn Majah 3029 (Abu Usamah from 'Awf) has it as a public address: 'يا أيها الناس إياكم والغلو في الدين...'. Also Musnad Ahmad.

12:21.ar: وَقَالَ ٱلَّذِي ٱشۡتَرَىٰهُ مِن مِّصۡرَ لِٱمۡرَأَتِهِۦٓ أَكۡرِمِي مَثۡوَىٰهُ عَسَىٰٓ أَن يَنفَعَنَآ أَوۡ نَتَّخِذَهُۥ وَلَدࣰ اۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ مَكَّنَّا لِيُوسُفَ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَلِنُعَلِّمَهُۥ مِن تَأۡوِيلِ ٱلۡأَحَادِيثِۚ وَٱللَّهُ غَالِبٌ عَلَىٰٓ أَمۡرِهِۦ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَ ٱلنَّاسِ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
12:21.en: And the one from Egypt who bought him said to his wife, "Make his residence comfortable. Perhaps he will benefit us, or we will adopt him as a son." And thus, We established Joseph in the land that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah is predominant over His affair, but most of the people do not know

12:22.ar: وَلَمَّا بَلَغَ أَشُدَّهُۥٓ ءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ حُكۡمࣰ ا وَعِلۡمࣰ اۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نَجۡزِي ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ
12:22.en: And when Joseph reached maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge. And thus We reward the doers of good

12:23.ar: وَرَٰوَدَتۡهُ ٱلَّتِي هُوَ فِي بَيۡتِهَا عَن نَّفۡسِهِۦ وَغَلَّقَتِ ٱلۡأَبۡوَٰبَ وَقَالَتۡ هَيۡتَ لَكَۚ قَالَ مَعَاذَ ٱللَّهِۖ إِنَّهُۥ رَبِّيٓ أَحۡسَنَ مَثۡوَايَۖ إِنَّهُۥ لَا يُفۡلِحُ ٱلظَّٰلِمُونَ
12:23.en: And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him. She closed the doors and said, "Come, you." He said, "[I seek] the refuge of Allah. Indeed, he is my master, who has made good my residence. Indeed, wrongdoers will not succeed

12:24.ar: وَلَقَدۡ هَمَّتۡ بِهِۦۖ وَهَمَّ بِهَا لَوۡلَآ أَن رَّءَا بُرۡهَٰنَ رَبِّهِۦۚ كَذَٰلِكَ لِنَصۡرِفَ عَنۡهُ ٱلسُّوٓءَ وَٱلۡفَحۡشَآءَۚ إِنَّهُۥ مِنۡ عِبَادِنَا ٱلۡمُخۡلَصِينَ
12:24.en: And she certainly determined [to seduce] him, and he would have inclined to her had he not seen the proof of his Lord. And thus [it was] that We should avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our chosen servants

12:25.ar: وَٱسۡتَبَقَا ٱلۡبَابَ وَقَدَّتۡ قَمِيصَهُۥ مِن دُبُرࣲ وَأَلۡفَيَا سَيِّدَهَا لَدَا ٱلۡبَابِۚ قَالَتۡ مَا جَزَآءُ مَنۡ أَرَادَ بِأَهۡلِكَ سُوٓءًا إِلَّآ أَن يُسۡجَنَ أَوۡ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمࣱ‏
12:25.en: And they both raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from the back, and they found her husband at the door. She said, "What is the recompense of one who intended evil for your wife but that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment

12:26.ar: قَالَ هِيَ رَٰوَدَتۡنِي عَن نَّفۡسِيۚ وَشَهِدَ شَاهِدࣱ مِّنۡ أَهۡلِهَآ إِن كَانَ قَمِيصُهُۥ قُدَّ مِن قُبُلࣲ فَصَدَقَتۡ وَهُوَ مِنَ ٱلۡكَٰذِبِينَ
12:26.en: [Joseph] said, "It was she who sought to seduce me." And a witness from her family testified. "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth, and he is of the liars

12:27.ar: وَإِن كَانَ قَمِيصُهُۥ قُدَّ مِن دُبُرࣲ فَكَذَبَتۡ وَهُوَ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰدِقِينَ
12:27.en: But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful

12:28.ar: فَلَمَّا رَءَا قَمِيصَهُۥ قُدَّ مِن دُبُرࣲ قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ مِن كَيۡدِكُنَّۖ إِنَّ كَيۡدَكُنَّ عَظِيمࣱ‏
12:28.en: So when her husband saw his shirt torn from the back, he said, "Indeed, it is of the women's plan. Indeed, your plan is great

12:29.ar: يُوسُفُ أَعۡرِضۡ عَنۡ هَٰذَاۚ وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرِي لِذَنۢبِكِۖ إِنَّكِ كُنتِ مِنَ ٱلۡخَاطِـِٔينَ
12:29.en: Joseph, ignore this. And, [my wife], ask forgiveness for your sin. Indeed, you were of the sinful

12:37.ar: قَالَ لَا يَأۡتِيكُمَا طَعَامࣱ تُرۡزَقَانِهِۦٓ إِلَّا نَبَّأۡتُكُمَا بِتَأۡوِيلِهِۦ قَبۡلَ أَن يَأۡتِيَكُمَاۚ ذَٰلِكُمَا مِمَّا عَلَّمَنِي رَبِّيٓۚ إِنِّي تَرَكۡتُ مِلَّةَ قَوۡمࣲ لَّا يُؤۡمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَهُم بِٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ هُمۡ كَٰفِرُونَ
12:37.en: He said, "You will not receive food that is provided to you except that I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is from what my Lord has taught me. Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah, and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers

12:38.ar: وَٱتَّبَعۡتُ مِلَّةَ ءَابَآءِيٓ إِبۡرَٰهِيمَ وَإِسۡحَٰقَ وَيَعۡقُوبَۚ مَا كَانَ لَنَآ أَن نُّشۡرِكَ بِٱللَّهِ مِن شَيۡءࣲۚ ذَٰلِكَ مِن فَضۡلِ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡنَا وَعَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَ ٱلنَّاسِ لَا يَشۡكُرُونَ
12:38.en: And I have followed the religion of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. And it was not for us to associate anything with Allah. That is from the favor of Allah upon us and upon the people, but most of the people are not grateful

12:39.ar: يَٰصَٰحِبَيِ ٱلسِّجۡنِ ءَأَرۡبَابࣱ مُّتَفَرِّقُونَ خَيۡرٌ أَمِ ٱللَّهُ ٱلۡوَٰحِدُ ٱلۡقَهَّارُ
12:39.en: O [my] two companions of prison, are separate lords better or Allah, the One, the Prevailing

105:1.ar: أَلَمۡ تَرَ كَيۡفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصۡحَٰبِ ٱلۡفِيلِ
105:1.en: Have you not considered, [O Muhammad], how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant

7Xgg9ido_Ks.title: Arabic Tafseer: Surah Yusuf (12:22-29)
7Xgg9ido_Ks.one_line: Yusuf and the wife of al-Aziz: every cause of temptation gathered, yet he refused because he had already seen his Lord's proof.
7Xgg9ido_Ks.summary: The sheikh resumes the episode of Yusuf and the wife of al-Aziz and lists every factor that made falling into zina easy: Yusuf was a slave with no reputation to lose, a young man, behind locked doors, pursued rather than pursuing, dependent on her power, and she was young and beautiful. Yet the only question for a believer is whether an act pleases Allah. Yusuf's answer gives three barriers: seeking refuge in Allah, loyalty to the man who honoured him, and the universal rule that wrongdoers never succeed. From this he argues that character is fixed and does not rise and fall with circumstances. His central point is verse 24: Yusuf did not incline to her because he had already seen his Lord's proof, a certainty of mind and heart built over his life, not a vision in the moment, and he rejects Isra'iliyyat to the contrary. He separates inclination, intention and wishing, explains that zina has preliminaries, and distinguishes the man who avoids sin from conviction from the one who simply lacks opportunity. He warns against reading tafsir or hadith without a teacher, then explains the race to the door, the torn shirt, the accusation and the witness whose forensic reasoning cleared Yusuf. He asks parents to start with belief so children reach that certainty.

outline.heading: Opening
Recap: Yusuf and the wife of al-Aziz
outline.gist: He returns to the episode of Zulaykha begun last week and the real difficulty in understanding it.

outline.heading: Given judgement and knowledge, yet a slave
outline.gist: Yusuf reached maturity with strong reasoning and knowledge from his father, but on paper he was a slave.

outline.heading: The man called by a woman of status and beauty
outline.gist: The hadith of the seven under Allah's shade alludes to Yusuf's stand.

outline.heading: First cause: no reputation at stake
outline.gist: As a slave nobody would hold him to account, so fear for his name could not restrain him.

outline.heading: Second cause: youth
outline.gist: A young man has less control over desire than a mature adult.

outline.heading: Third cause: the closed doors
outline.gist: She hid him from every eye, removing his natural shyness and fear of exposure.

outline.heading: Fourth cause: she pursued him
outline.gist: She sought him; he did not seek her.

outline.heading: Fifth cause: his life depended on her
outline.gist: She held power in the house and threatened him; she was also young and beautiful, close to his age.

outline.heading: Every cause gathered, while people today chase sin
outline.gist: Today people work around every barrier to reach the haram; Yusuf had it handed to him.

outline.heading: No risk to him, and even leverage
outline.gist: She was the one who feared scandal, so he could even have used it against her.

outline.heading: The only question: does it please Allah?
outline.gist: The believer is spared endless calculations of risk and cost; if it angers Allah the matter is closed.

outline.heading: Rawadathu, ghallaqat, hayta lak
outline.gist: The verse describes the scene clearly in chaste language; she had prepared herself for him.

outline.heading: A proof against men until the Last Day
outline.gist: Because it happened, no man can claim he had no way out of zina.

outline.heading: Ma'adh Allah: an immediate refusal
outline.gist: He rejects readings that suggest Yusuf weakened; his answer was instant.

outline.heading: First barrier: refuge in Allah
outline.gist: He seeks refuge in Allah from what angers Him.

outline.heading: Second barrier: loyalty to the one who honoured him
outline.gist: Al-Aziz honoured him; Yusuf keeps the loyalty his own brothers denied their father.

outline.heading: Character does not fluctuate
outline.gist: Character has no ebb and flow; once adopted it is kept until one meets Allah, and he admits he does not yet know how to teach this to youth.

outline.heading: Generous only when rich is an opportunist
outline.gist: The amount may change with circumstances, but the trait itself stays constant.

outline.heading: The only story told unbroken
outline.gist: Surah Yusuf tells one story start to finish, unlike the stories of Musa or Ibrahim.

outline.heading: Steadfastness is the lesson
outline.gist: The story is not only about a man invited to sin but about staying the same under every pressure.

outline.heading: Third barrier: wrongdoers never succeed
outline.gist: A general understanding of existence: tyrants end in the rubbish heap of history.

outline.heading: Source of his strength: his father's teaching
outline.gist: His values came from Yaqub's upbringing and the knowledge Allah gave him.

outline.heading: Wa laqad hammat bihi: where to pause
outline.gist: One should stop after her intention, since joining the phrases misleads the listener.

outline.heading: The proof was seen earlier, not in the moment
outline.gist: Reading it as a sudden vision contradicts the previous verse; the Quran explains itself.

outline.heading: Law la: prevention through a prior cause
outline.gist: Because he had seen the proof, inclining to her never happened.

outline.heading: Inclination, intention and wishful thinking
outline.gist: Hamm precedes intention; intention is firm resolve; a wish carries no reward or sin.

outline.heading: A burhan is not seen with the eyes
outline.gist: Burhan means a rational proof, seen by mind and heart.

outline.heading: Rejecting the Isra'iliyyat
outline.gist: Stories of him seeing his father's face contradict the Quran and are rejected.

outline.heading: Zina has preliminaries: fortify yourself beforehand
outline.gist: Nobody falls suddenly; it comes step by step through eyes, ears and wishes, hence the command not to approach zina.

outline.heading: Evidence from his words in prison
outline.gist: Months later he declares he follows the creed of his fathers, showing his long-held certainty.

outline.heading: Seeing as the Prophet saw the Elephant army
outline.gist: The Prophet saw what happened to Abraha's army through reports and its blind survivors, not with his own eyes.

outline.heading: She certainly intended; he would have, but for the proof
outline.gist: The lam and qad confirm her intent; he was protected beforehand.

outline.heading: Linasrifa 'anhu: equipped to turn evil away
outline.gist: Allah did not keep temptation from him; He prepared him to turn it away himself.

outline.heading: Among Our devoted servants
outline.gist: Al-mukhlasin are those Allah purified for Himself by filling their hearts with sincerity.

outline.heading: Two kinds of people who avoid sin
outline.gist: One saw the proof of his Lord; the other simply lacks opportunity; the same holds for haram money.

outline.heading: The most important phrase in the surah
outline.gist: Character only comes from seeing the proof; many of us are fine only because Allah has covered us.

outline.heading: How do we instil this in our children?
outline.gist: He asks openly how to bring this fortification to hearts and minds.

outline.heading: Three barriers against a thousand excuses
outline.gist: Religion, loyalty and wisdom each stood as a dam between Yusuf and sin.

outline.heading: Interpretations that cast doubt on Yusuf
outline.gist: Muddying a deep verse turns people away from its meaning, which is Iblis's work.

outline.heading: Encyclopedic tafsirs and weak reports
outline.gist: Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi collect every report with chains so scholars can know the weak ones.

outline.heading: Read hadith and tafsir with a teacher
outline.gist: Without the tools of Arabic and Quranic sciences, reading alone leads to confusion, as social media shows.

outline.heading: Seeing the proof means certainty in promise and threat
outline.gist: Certainty extends to Allah's promise of paradise and threat of fire, which protects the believer.

outline.heading: Begin with belief
outline.gist: To protect ourselves and our children, start with creed and knowing Allah's majesty.

outline.heading: Question: the one who avoids sin for lack of chance
outline.gist: He declines to rule on the second kind, as scholars have long kept silent out of fear.

outline.heading: The frightening 'if' that Allah knows
outline.gist: Allah knows what people would do if tested; ask for safety and seek the proof of your Lord.

outline.heading: The race to the door and the torn shirt
outline.gist: Recitation of the verse with a note on reading qamis correctly.

outline.heading: Istabaqa: the same word as the brothers' race
outline.gist: His brothers raced to destroy him; now he races away from sin.

outline.heading: Qadd and the meaning of qamis
outline.gist: Qadd is tearing and keeping the torn piece; qamis is any garment worn over the shoulders.

outline.heading: Alfaya sayyidaha: surprised at the last door
outline.gist: Sayyid shows her husband was older and that she was young.

outline.heading: Her accusation and the trials ahead
outline.gist: She immediately accuses him; the story will still test Yusuf's word.

outline.heading: Hiya rawadatni: Yusuf defends himself
outline.gist: Recitation of the next verses.

outline.heading: Two claims before al-Aziz
outline.gist: She claims assault and he says she seduced him; al-Aziz was not alone at the door.

outline.heading: Who the witness was
outline.gist: A relative of hers, likely the head of police, while al-Aziz oversaw the treasury.

outline.heading: Forensic reasoning from the shirt
outline.gist: A tear in front means he advanced; a tear behind means he fled.

outline.heading: Why her claim was tested first
outline.gist: In such cases the claim of the woman is examined first; an unmarried man alone with a woman is already blameworthy.

outline.heading: Surah Yusuf's many sciences
outline.gist: The surah contains criminal investigation and economic planning, and Yusuf learned from this man too.

outline.heading: Inna kaydakunna 'azim
outline.gist: The witness concludes it was her scheme, tells Yusuf to drop it and her to seek forgiveness.

outline.heading: Outro

l8e_Lt8IZ8M.title: The Implications of Knowing: Moral Integrity (Part 2)
l8e_Lt8IZ8M.one_line: Second khutbah on moral integrity: knowing Allah must produce ethics, hypocrisy is a moral failure, and obedience is loyalty to the Creator.
l8e_Lt8IZ8M.summary: Second khutbah on moral integrity, the first implication of knowing Allah, in his series on what knowing God must produce. He opens with the verse on the hypocrites and the problem of useless information: knowledge of Allah, His Messenger and His Book must translate into something measurable, and bad religiosity comes from lacking this. Hypocrisy is an ethical failure, saying one thing and doing another, and the hadith of the hypocrite's signs shows it: lying, breaking promises, betraying pacts and abandoning all ethics in a dispute. The relationship with Allah is itself ethical. He created you from nothing, needs nothing and cannot be repaid, so gratitude, loyalty and obedience are the only ethical response; turning your back on Him is a moral breach. The same logic places parents second, which is why the Quran pairs worship of Allah with kindness to them. Prayer, fasting and zakah are rituals in form but ethics at their core, and separating fiqh from akhlaq is meaningless. The straight path of al-Fatihah is istiqama, doing the right thing in every situation without corruption or back doors. He closes by asking Muslims to bring this ethic back into homes, schools, work and relationships and to endure the cost of standing by it.

outline.heading: Opening
The hypocrites' verse: what does knowing Allah mean?
outline.gist: He recites the verse on the hypocrites, men and women alike, who enjoin wrong, forbid right and forgot Allah, and asks what knowing Allah is supposed to mean in practice.

outline.heading: An overload of useless information
outline.gist: Modern life fills the mind with information that never changes or helps us, clogging it until things that matter fall out.

outline.heading: Knowledge of Allah must be measurable
outline.gist: Knowing that Allah is One, that Muhammad is His messenger and that the Book is his legacy must translate into something clear and measurable. All bad religiosity comes from lacking moral integrity, by far the first implication of knowing Him.

outline.heading: Hypocrisy is an ethical failure
outline.gist: Hypocrisy must be understood so one can stay away from it, and at its core it is ethical: saying one thing and doing another, enjoining wrong and forbidding right.

outline.heading: The hypocrite's signs: ethics drop in a dispute
outline.gist: He lies when he speaks, breaks his promises and betrays his pacts, and once you disagree with him every ethical limit falls away: he uses any back way to harm you.

outline.heading: Created from nothing by One who needs nothing
outline.gist: The relationship with Allah is itself ethical. He created you from nothing; you want to repay a giver by meeting his needs, but He has none, and you could never repay existence, which everyone wants.

outline.heading: Turning your back on Him is an ethical breach
outline.gist: Since you cannot repay Him, the only ethical response is to be grateful, loyal and to listen to what He says. Saying He gave me everything but I do not care is a lack of morality, not only a religious failure.

outline.heading: He also offers the only path to prosperity
outline.gist: Beyond creating you, the way of life He offers is the only route to prosperity in this life and the next, and He will resurrect you to an eternity of bliss and nearness you did nothing to earn; refusing that is unethical.

outline.heading: Not a relationship between equals
outline.gist: There is no argument or objection a person could raise: he is not His equal, everything comes from Him, and the relationship is of a different kind altogether.

outline.heading: Parents come second, after Allah
outline.gist: Obedience and submission are ethical before they are rituals. The Quran pairs worshipping Allah alone with kindness to parents because after Him they gave you the most; logically it cannot be otherwise.

outline.heading: Love of the Prophet and all of Islam rest on ethics
outline.gist: Umar was told his love for the Prophet had to exceed his love for himself, an ethical duty. Everything in Islam, prayer and kinship ties included, is a logical conclusion of moral integrity, which means setting aside your own interests and agendas, and that is always hard.

outline.heading: Interlude
Knowing Allah produces nothing but akhlaq
outline.gist: In Arabic: the first result of knowing Allah is steadfast character; obedience, response to His command and even the name Muslim are ethical responses, because no one can be given everything and owe nothing.

outline.heading: Obedience is the only repayment
outline.gist: We cannot repay Him and He needs nothing we own, so He gave commands and obedience became loyalty to the One who created, provided and guided. Prayer, fasting and zakah are rituals, but ethical at their core.

outline.heading: Nothing in the deen stands apart from akhlaq
outline.gist: That is why kindness to parents is the first command after tawhid. Separating fiqh or rituals from akhlaq is meaningless; the whole deen follows the ethical pyramid the Prophet brought, and nothing matters more or is less understood today.

outline.heading: The straight path is istiqama: always doing the right thing
outline.gist: Muslims ask for the straight path at least seventeen times a day, and no one takes it literally. Istiqama is absolute integrity: doing the right thing in every situation even when it is inconvenient or costs a goal. Everyone knows what the right thing is; the path is not lying to yourself, finding no back door and refusing corruption.

outline.heading: Worship is the right thing; then be upright
outline.gist: This is not his personal reading but the path Muslims are commanded to walk. Worshipping Allah is itself among the right things, since He created you and gave you everything; the Prophet said: say I believe in Allah, then be upright.

outline.heading: People are mines
outline.gist: The Prophet said people are like mines of different metals: the best of them before Islam are the best of them in Islam once they understand.

outline.heading: Late converts who were ahead of everyone
outline.gist: Knowing Allah corrects and completes an ethical code that is already there; companions who accepted Islam late were ahead because they had moral integrity. That must come back into hearts, homes, schools and work.

outline.heading: Endure the cost of standing by your ethics
outline.gist: Learn to bear the pain of not following personal needs or agendas, taking no shortcuts and telling no lies; that is what it means to be Muslim, even while the wealthy and powerful get ahead through their lack of morals.

outline.heading: Outro

0aoMma6bqsQ.title: From Populations to Communities: Financial Centralization
0aoMma6bqsQ.one_line: On the anniversary of the London attack, a call to stop idling as a population and centralize zakat, charity and endowments.
0aoMma6bqsQ.summary: The sheikh continues his series on how Muslims in the West move from a population to a community by centralizing four things: social, financial, political and religious life. Marking five years since the attack on a Muslim family in London, he recalls hearing the news and says Muslims grieve for three days and then carry the lessons forward. After thirteen years in the city, he sees growth in numbers and institutions but no real progress in organization or unity, and argues that the Prophet left Mecca precisely because the ummah needed to organize. A recent death of a young attendee reminds him how fragile life is: stop postponing the right thing, because sincere intention while there is still time is enough. He warns against short memory, recalling the weekly death counts from Gaza that people stopped caring about. In the second part he turns to finances. Zuhd is not poverty but taking little for yourself while using wealth for others. Muslims in the city lack neither money nor numbers, only a way to centralize zakat, voluntary charity and waqf. He cites Abu Bakr's insistence on central zakat and the creativity of historical endowments, urges everyone to create a personal waqf, and wants spending driven by need rather than fundraising skill.

outline.heading: Opening
From population to community: four centralizations
outline.gist: A community, the building block of the ummah, needs something centralized; Muslims in the West are still populations.

outline.heading: Five years since the London attack
outline.gist: He recalls where he was when he heard the news and how it shattered the belief that this could not happen here.

outline.heading: Grieve three days, then carry the lessons
outline.gist: The date should remind us how far we still have to go to secure safety and a voice for future generations.

outline.heading: Thirteen years with little real progress
outline.gist: Numbers and institutions grew, but proportionally we are not more organized or united.

outline.heading: Think bigger: belonging to an ummah
outline.gist: Stop wasting time on internal politics; our task is to introduce Allah to people, which needs organization.

outline.heading: Why the Prophet left Mecca
outline.gist: He left his birthplace, his deepest scar, because the ummah could only organize in Medina.

outline.heading: Thirty nationalities, one testimony
outline.gist: Agreement on la ilaha illa Allah is enough to overlook every other difference.

outline.heading: Life is fragile: stop postponing
outline.gist: Tragedy forces us to see that nothing is guaranteed and the right thing must be first on our list.

outline.heading: A sincere intention now is enough
outline.gist: Until the sun rises from the west, anyone still breathing can turn around.

outline.heading: Short memory: the forgotten death counts
outline.gist: We once counted Gaza's dead every week; now people want light talks and short khutbahs.

outline.heading: Do not become desensitized
outline.gist: He begs young people not to live for the next trip and weekend.

outline.heading: Interlude
Goals of the Islamic economic system
outline.gist: Use resources well, ensure no one is in need, and strengthen the community and ummah.

outline.heading: Zuhd is not poverty
outline.gist: Pursue wealth so you are not at others' mercy, but take only what you need for yourself.

outline.heading: Three kinds of wealth, none centralized
outline.gist: Zakat, sadaqah and waqf: the city has money and numbers but no central use for them.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr and central zakat
outline.gist: He fought those who withheld zakat from the centre because financial unity saved the ummah.

outline.heading: The creativity of endowments
outline.gist: Waqfs once paid people to speak hopefully outside a dying patient's room.

outline.heading: Make a waqf in your own life
outline.gist: Dedicate a table, a workday or a sum; take care of the local community first so something remains.

outline.heading: Need, not fundraising skill
outline.gist: Money should go where specialists say it is needed; paying for a masjid is paying for yourself.

outline.heading: What is missing: will and leadership
outline.gist: Everyone agrees in principle; what lacks is willpower, organization and setting egos aside.

outline.heading: Outro

DVdbpHob020.title: Tafseer of Surat An-Nazi'at, Part 2 (79:15-33)
DVdbpHob020.one_line: Musa and Pharaoh as a study of the untamed nafs, then the cosmos verses that humble us and preserve our self-worth.
DVdbpHob020.summary: The sheikh places An-Nazi'at in the final cluster of surahs as the one about the tool for living a belief: the nafs, which is both the problem and the solution. He explains the short Musa passage. The valley of Tuwa, from a root for folding something away, is where hidden realities were unveiled to Musa, starting with the warning that the battle is first inside. Pharaoh's tughyan is oppression of others born of inner arrogance. Yet Allah's first offer to the worst dictator, a man who killed children, was purification and guidance leading to khashyah, which he defines as a mix of fear of just punishment, respect and love, unlike fear of people. He argues every great conflict reduces to swollen egos, illustrated by Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik passing rule to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. Pharaoh rejected a sign he knew was true, the essence of kufr, and declared himself the highest lord. The lesson is that the same monster sleeps in anyone given enough power; the nafs's trick is convincing you that you and it are one. The cosmos verses then humble us, while their final verse says all of it was made as provision for us. Tazkiyah is accepting both truths, which ends the struggle to prove you are more or fear you are less.

outline.heading: Opening
The final cluster and the pillars of a belief
outline.gist: These surahs summarize the Quran; An-Naba gave the narrative of existence and An-Nazi'at gives the tool to live it.

outline.heading: The nafs: obstacle or salvation
outline.gist: The same engine takes you where you want if tamed or where it wants if not; the answers lie within you.

outline.heading: Recap: oaths by souls and the Day of Judgment
outline.gist: The first paragraph showed different kinds of souls and how hearts and eyes react on that day.

outline.heading: Musa and Pharaoh, the Quran's most told story
outline.gist: A short version shaped to serve the surah's focus on the nafs.

outline.heading: Hal ataka: an invitation to listen
outline.gist: The rhetorical question draws the listener into the story.

outline.heading: Where the sacred valley lies
outline.gist: Musa first heard Allah on his way back to Egypt, near Sinai.

outline.heading: Tuwa: the valley of what was folded away
outline.gist: The name points to hidden realities of existence unveiled to Musa there.

outline.heading: What Musa heard first
outline.gist: Take off your shoes, worship Me, pray and prepare for the hidden Hour; do not let those who follow desire divert you.

outline.heading: The battle begins inside
outline.gist: Whoever conquers his nafs can conquer anything; whoever fails there loses in the long run despite worldly success.

outline.heading: Tagha: oppression and inner arrogance
outline.gist: The same word describes the people of the fire earlier in the surah: oppression of others and arrogance inside.

outline.heading: Pharaoh, the Hyksos and the enslaved Israelites
outline.gist: Bani Isra'il, allies of the Hyksos, were enslaved after them, which is why Surah Yusuf says king and not Pharaoh.

outline.heading: The epitome of dictatorship
outline.gist: Pharaoh is the Quran's model of the tyrant.

outline.heading: Hal laka ila: the language of an offer
outline.gist: The phrasing presents something in the listener's own interest.

outline.heading: Tazakka, and the fight over a word
outline.gist: Whatever one thinks of the later term tasawwuf, the Quranic concept of tazkiyah must not be lost.

outline.heading: The hadith of Jibril: the third bucket
outline.gist: The religion is belief, practice and the inner life of ihsan, not just the first two.

outline.heading: Why offer purification to a tyrant
outline.gist: He finds it striking that a man deserving the sword was first offered self-purification.

outline.heading: The killing of children and Musa in the Nile
outline.gist: Pharaoh's dream led him to kill newborn boys; Allah had Musa raised in his own house.

outline.heading: The offer: fix what is inside
outline.gist: His problem was not politics or strategy but the monster within; tame it and be guided to your Lord.

outline.heading: Khashyah is more than fear
outline.gist: It combines fear of just punishment, respect and love; scholars are those who truly revere Allah.

outline.heading: Fearing people versus revering Allah
outline.gist: We fear people's injustice and resent them; with Allah we fear only receiving no more than we deserve.

outline.heading: Haybah: reverence among people
outline.gist: Everyone has a figure they feared to disappoint; societies without such figures collapse.

outline.heading: Every conflict comes down to ego
outline.gist: Behind wars stand people too arrogant to back down; those who seek office are usually the opposite of what is needed.

outline.heading: Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik's last decision
outline.gist: Troubled at the end of his life, he gave succession to someone his nafs had no stake in.

outline.heading: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz's short reign
outline.gist: One moment of sincerity in a ruler changed the trajectory of the ummah; his reign is worth studying.

outline.heading: Pharaoh was still salvageable
outline.gist: Musa was told to use soft words; salvation started with taming the inside, not changing laws.

outline.heading: Recitation and the silent alif
outline.gist: Reciting the rest of the paragraph with a note on the alif read only when stopping.

outline.heading: The great sign and the magicians
outline.gist: The staff and the shining hand; the illusionists believed first because they knew a trick when they saw one.

outline.heading: Kufr: refusing what makes sense to you
outline.gist: Disbelief is rejecting what you yourself see as true, usually for ego.

outline.heading: He turned away and gathered his people
outline.gist: He pursued his own plan and called everyone to hear his claim.

outline.heading: It could be you: the sleeping monster
outline.gist: The story is not to mock Pharaoh; anyone given enough power could reveal the same ugliness.

outline.heading: I am your lord most high
outline.gist: He said openly what earlier rulers only implied, using a name that belongs to Allah alone.

outline.heading: Seized for the last and the first
outline.gist: His claim deserved punishment before even his oppression did; none of us is beyond it.

outline.heading: A lesson for whoever reveres
outline.gist: Reverence lets you see how far an untamed nafs can go.

outline.heading: The nafs's biggest trick
outline.gist: It convinces you that its wants are yours; it loves you but does not know your good, so tame it rather than hate it.

outline.heading: Recitation of the third paragraph
outline.gist: He closes the Musa passage and recites the cosmos verses.

outline.heading: Are you harder to create, or the heaven?
outline.gist: A humbling question about strength in every sense.

outline.heading: The scale of the cosmos
outline.gist: Light years and billions of galaxies are beyond comprehension; the heaven is raised and balanced.

outline.heading: Night, day and the smoothed earth
outline.gist: Daha means smoothing something oval.

outline.heading: Water, pasture and mountains: humbled
outline.gist: Every verse reminds him how small he is.

outline.heading: All of it provision for you and your cattle
outline.gist: Everything greater than you was created to serve you.

outline.heading: Tazkiyah is not self-hatred
outline.gist: It is accepting the truth, which fixes your value so it neither rises nor falls.

outline.heading: Neither truth needs your agreement
outline.gist: You are small and all was made for you; being told you are more is as harmful as being told you are less.

outline.heading: Preserving self-worth
outline.gist: If you feel more, read the first verses; if you feel less, read the last.

outline.heading: Outro

CsuSgyWXi3Y.one_line: Through the companion who vowed to stand in the sun, stay silent and fast, the Prophet shows no one may invent new worship.
CsuSgyWXi3Y.summary: The sheikh opens a short series on moderation (wasatiyyah), a value he has been working on with the mentorship groups. He uses the hadith of a companion the Prophet noticed standing in the sun while others sat. The man had vowed to stand and never sit, to avoid shade, to stop speaking and to fast. The sheikh stresses that this was a good man who simply wanted to get closer to Allah by giving up comforts. The Prophet told him to sit, take the shade and speak, and to complete his fast. The point is that the man had added new items to the roster of worship. Silence as devotion existed in earlier scripture, as with Maryam, but not in this religion. Fasting is a real act of worship, so that part stayed. The sheikh draws the rule that no one has the right to add acts of worship to Islam: the Prophet already taught exactly how to please Allah, and invented devotions cause harm, open the door to extremism and empty the religion of its essence. He notes that this was one of the rare areas where the Prophet became sharply assertive, and asks listeners to stay within the forms of worship they were given.

hadith.gist: A man (Abu Isra'il) vowed to stand in the sun without sitting, shade or speech while fasting; the Prophet ordered him to sit, take shade, speak and complete his fast.

full.full_ar: يروي الإمام البخاري في صحيحه (6704) قال: حَدَّثَنَا مُوسَى بْنُ إِسْمَاعِيلَ، حَدَّثَنَا وُهَيْبٌ، حَدَّثَنَا أَيُّوبُ، عَنْ عِكْرِمَةَ، عَنِ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ، قال: «بَيْنَا النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَخْطُبُ إِذَا هُوَ بِرَجُلٍ قَائِمٍ فَسَأَلَ عَنْهُ فَقَالُوا أَبُو إِسْرَائِيلَ نَذَرَ أَنْ يَقُومَ وَلاَ يَقْعُدَ وَلاَ يَسْتَظِلَّ وَلاَ يَتَكَلَّمَ وَيَصُومَ. فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم “مُرْهُ فَلْيَتَكَلَّمْ وَلْيَسْتَظِلَّ وَلْيَقْعُدْ وَلْيُتِمَّ صَوْمَهُ”»
full.full_en: Imam al-Bukhari narrates in his Sahih (6704): Musa ibn Isma'il narrated to us from Wuhayb, from Ayyub, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "While the Prophet (peace be upon him) was giving a sermon, he saw a man standing, and asked about him. They said: This is Abu Isra'il. He vowed to stand and not sit, not take shade, not speak, and to fast. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Tell him to speak, take shade, sit, and complete his fast.'"

full.isnad_en: Musa ibn Isma'il, from Wuhayb, from Ayyub, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas
full.ar_block: يروي الإمام البخاري في صحيحه، بسند صحيح، عن عبد الله بن عباس رضي الله عنهما قال: «بَيْنَا النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَخْطُبُ إِذَا هُوَ بِرَجُلٍ قَائِمٍ فَسَأَلَ عَنْهُ فَقَالُوا أَبُو إِسْرَائِيلَ نَذَرَ أَنْ يَقُومَ وَلاَ يَقْعُدَ وَلاَ يَسْتَظِلَّ وَلاَ يَتَكَلَّمَ وَيَصُومَ. فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم “مُرْهُ فَلْيَتَكَلَّمْ وَلْيَسْتَظِلَّ وَلْيَقْعُدْ وَلْيُتِمَّ صَوْمَهُ”»
full.en_block: Imam al-Bukhari narrates in his Sahih, with a sahih chain, that Abdullah ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "While the Prophet (peace be upon him) was giving a sermon, he saw a man standing, and asked about him. They said: This is Abu Isra'il. He vowed to stand and not sit, not take shade, not speak, and to fast. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Tell him to speak, take shade, sit, and complete his fast.'"
full.grade: Sahih (al-Bukhari). Al-Bukhari adds a mursal route (Abd al-Wahhab from Ayyub from Ikrimah from the Prophet) as a supporting note; the connected chain through Ibn Abbas is the main one.

9:60.en: Zakah expenditures are only for the poor and for the needy and for those employed to collect [zakah] and for bringing hearts together [for Islam] and for freeing captives [or slaves] and for those in debt and for the cause of Allah and for the [stranded] traveler - an obligation [imposed] by Allah. VsTpEFBZepg.title: Funds Network and the Philosophy of Giving Local
VsTpEFBZepg.one_line: A Funds Network co-founder argues zakat should be collected and spent in the community where wealth is earned, and explains how his organization does it.
VsTpEFBZepg.summary: The guest, a dentist and co-founder of Funds Network, a sister organization of the masjid, argues for giving zakat locally. He starts from the size of London's Muslim community and the likelihood that most will spend their lives in Canada, then grounds the idea in the Prophet's instruction to Mu'adh that zakat be taken from a community's rich and returned to its poor, and the hadith about sleeping full while a neighbour is hungry. He stresses that zakat is precise in amount, payers and the eight recipient categories, and that centralized finances, knowledge and ethics have been the sources of Muslim strength. Using Canadian data on refugees, food costs and deep poverty, he shows real local need. He criticizes charities run like businesses with paid staff, heavy marketing and a bias toward attractive overseas projects, and urges donors to read charities' public financial statements and hold institutions accountable. Funds Network supports about 50 to 60 recommended families monthly, distributes all Ramadan zakat and Eid meat, and invests a share of the collectors' portion in real estate for the next generation. Questions from the audience on charitable status, audits and screening follow.

outline.gist: Most Muslims here will live their whole lives in Canada, so the community must build institutions and invest for the next generation.

outline.heading: Taken from their rich, given to their poor
outline.gist: The Prophet's instruction to Mu'adh in Yemen keeps zakat within the community rather than sending it to the centre.

outline.heading: Zakat is precise, not a general donation
outline.gist: A fixed share from set wealth and people to set recipients; it cannot be spent on buildings or general masjid costs.

outline.heading: Three sources of Muslim strength
outline.gist: Centralized finances through zakat, knowledge and ethics have sustained Muslims and are each under attack.

outline.heading: The hungry neighbour
outline.gist: The hadith denying full faith to one who sleeps full while his neighbour is hungry teaches attention to local surroundings.

outline.heading: The eight categories of zakat
outline.gist: The poor and needy, collectors, new Muslims, debtors, the stranded traveller and others, with a warning that collectors' share is not a blank cheque.

outline.heading: Is there poverty in Canada?
outline.gist: Poverty here is not only homelessness; lacking essentials such as technology and food security counts.

outline.heading: Refugees and the rising cost of living
outline.gist: About 27,000 refugees in London and a steep rise in food costs widen the gap between income and spending.

outline.heading: Deep poverty and its harms
outline.gist: The Canadian definition of deep poverty and its links to poor health, unemployment, crime and exploitation.

outline.heading: A volunteer model, not a business
outline.gist: Funds Network pays no staff and keeps full transparency; financial security comes before people can seek knowledge.

outline.heading: Supporting recommended families toward independence
outline.gist: Families are selected by recommendation; the young and able are pushed toward self-sufficiency while others will always need help.

outline.heading: Problems with charities run like businesses
outline.gist: Burnout, expensive paid marketing, large paid staff and a bias to attractive overseas projects; donors should read charities' public financial statements.

outline.heading: Serving the deen without contradicting it
outline.gist: Institutions must operate by the sunnah; donors should budget and start with local giving.

outline.heading: Long-term investment for the next generation
outline.gist: What will the community have in 25 to 35 years? Planting trees today for children to harvest.

outline.heading: Funding investment from the collectors' share
outline.gist: Answering whether zakat can be invested: the organization redirects its collectors' portion into investments, about 90,000 dollars so far.

outline.heading: Shared responsibility of institutions and donors
outline.gist: Institutions owe transparency and proper allocation; the public must ask questions and hold them accountable.

outline.heading: What Funds Network does
outline.gist: Monthly cash support of 300 to 500 dollars per family, Ramadan zakat of about 130,000 dollars fully distributed, and Eid meat for over 400 people.

outline.heading: Questions on charitable status and real estate
outline.gist: Audience questions on why it is not yet a registered charity given audit costs, and how the real estate investment works.

outline.heading: Screening against abuse
outline.gist: How recipients are checked when some people go from one institution to another.

outline.heading: Building your own community first
outline.gist: Your children will grow up here; if you cannot build your own community you cannot build any other.

outline.heading: Outro

A1X8QTA8XHQ.title: Post Isha Khaterah: The Three Marks of Success
A1X8QTA8XHQ.one_line: A hadith from Muslim redefines success as submission to Allah, sufficient provision, and contentment with what He gives.
A1X8QTA8XHQ.summary: The speaker presents the hadith in Sahih Muslim that the successful one is he who submits, is given just enough, and is made content by Allah with what he receives. He frames it not as a checklist but as a shift in how Muslims define success compared with the world. Submission closes the gap between the life we envision and the life that unfolds, a gap that breeds misery, by accepting Allah's decree as wiser. Sufficient provision is praised over abundance, supported by the hadith that whoever wakes safe, healthy and with his day's food has been given the whole world. Contentment is the perspective that keeps a person from tying happiness to the next milestone, since reaching a job or marriage gives a brief high before a return to baseline. As a practical application he teaches the dua asking Allah to provide what He sees fit and to make one content with it, said at the end of one's personal supplications.

outline.heading: A mindset shift on success
outline.gist: The hadith gives defining criteria for success rather than a checklist.

outline.heading: First criterion: submitting your will to Allah
outline.gist: Accepting Allah's decree bridges the gap between expected and actual reality that breeds misery.

outline.heading: Second criterion: just enough provision
outline.gist: Sufficiency, not abundance, is praised; safety, health and a day's food are like owning the world.

outline.heading: Third criterion: contentment
outline.gist: Milestones bring a brief high and a return to baseline; contentment is a perspective, not an arrival.

outline.heading: The dua of contentment
outline.gist: Ask for what you want, then ask Allah to provide what He sees fit and make you content with it.

outline.heading: Outro
